title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
也今日咸寧則是至仁被一時之億兆矣而何
道以洽之必其恩深懷保而厚澤首加於窮民
德普惠鮮而苛政不及於無告夫不虐可能也
無告而不虐則愛民之至矣持此心以撫綏天
下民尚有失所而不獲安者耶賢人至無盡若
難乎悉致也今日無遺則是登崇盡一時之豪
傑矣而何道以徠之必其賢有可舉雖側陋而
必揚才有可用雖世類而不拘夫不廢可能也
困窮而不廢則好士之至矣持此心以鼓舞天
===
下士尚有抱其道而甘於在野者耶是爲言爲
民爲賢勢若至渙而難萃而取言愛民好士道
則克盡而無虧此道盡而效自因之矣斯帝堯
之所獨能而我君臣所當交勉者也吁舜之克
艱亦可見矣雖然舜之爲君好察邇言則罔伏
矣好生洽民則不虐矣闢門求賢則不廢矣而
顧爲是退託者何哉蓋聖心至虛視己能恒若
未能此所以治益治而聖益聖也後世夜前席
以納言行小惠以愛民亟問餽而好士視此可
punctuated: 也。今日「咸寧」，則是至仁被一時之億兆矣，而何道以洽之？必其恩深懷保，而厚澤首加於窮民；德普惠鮮，而苛政不及於無告。夫不虐可能也，無告而不虐，則愛民之至矣。持此心以撫綏天下，民尚有失所而不獲安者耶？賢人至無盡，若難乎悉致也。今日「無遺」，則是登崇盡一時之豪傑矣，而何道以徠之？必其賢有可舉，雖側陋而必揚；才有可用，雖世類而不拘。夫不廢可能也，困窮而不廢，則好士之至矣。持此心以鼓舞天下，士尚有抱其道而甘於在野者耶？是爲言、爲民、爲賢，勢若至渙而難萃，而取言、愛民、好士，道則克盡而無虧，此道盡而效自因之矣。斯帝堯之所獨能，而我君臣所當交勉者也。吁！舜之克艱亦可見矣。雖然，舜之爲君，好察邇言則罔伏矣，好生洽民則不虐矣，闢門求賢則不廢矣，而顧爲是退託者何哉？蓋聖心至虛，視己能恒若未能，此所以治益治而聖益聖也。後世夜前席以納言，行小惠以愛民，亟問餽而好士，視此可
translation_en: …。 Now, when it says that "all the myriad regions were in repose," it means that the utmost benevolence covered the millions of people of that age; yet by what way did he pervade them with it? Surely his grace was deep in cherishing and protecting, so that his generous bounty was first bestowed upon the destitute; his virtue was universal in showing kindness to the widowers and needy, so that harsh governance never reached the helpless who had no one to appeal to. Now, not to oppress is something one might manage; but not to oppress the helpless is the utmost in loving the people. Holding fast to this mind in pacifying and soothing the empire, would there still be any among the people who lost their place and failed to obtain peace? Worthy men are utterly inexhaustible, so that it seems difficult to summon them all. Now, when it says that "none were left unengaged," it means that he elevated and honored all the outstanding talents of the age; yet by what way did he attract them? Surely when a man had worthiness that could be recommended, even if he was of humble and obscure station he was certain to be raised up; when a man had talent that could be employed, even regardless of his family background he was not restricted. Now, not to neglect is something one might manage; but not to neglect those in distress and poverty is the utmost in loving scholars. Holding fast to this mind in inspiring the empire, would there still be any among the scholars who clutched their Way to themselves and were content to remain in the wilderness? Thus, with regard to words, the people, and the worthy, their circumstances seem utterly scattered and hard to gather together; yet in adopting words, loving the people, and loving scholars, the Way was completely fulfilled without deficiency. When this Way was fulfilled, the results naturally followed from it. This is what Emperor Yao (Di Yao 帝堯) alone was able to do, and what we, sovereign and ministers, ought mutually to strive after. Ah! How Shun 舜 was able to recognize the difficulty of his task can also be seen here. Even so, in Shun's conduct as a ruler, he loved to examine near words, and thus nothing was hidden; his love of life pervaded the people, and thus he did not oppress; he threw open the doors to seek the worthy, and thus he did not neglect them. Why then did he nevertheless speak with such modest diffidence? It is because the sage's mind is utterly humble, always viewing what he is already able to do as if he were not yet able to do it; this is why his governance became ever more well-governed and his sageliness ever more sage. In later ages, those who edged forward on their mats at night to receive advice, practiced petty favors to love the people, or sent frequent inquiries and gifts to show fondness for scholars—compared with this, they may well…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
以少愧矣
自殷王中宗及高宗及祖甲及我周文王
茲四人迪哲
陳紹虞
同考試官訓導唐批發揮迪哲二字理精詞
練經義之最佳者宜錄以式
考試官訓導唐批得周公告成王之旨
考試官敎諭鄭批明實
大臣申言古人無逸之實惟行其所知而已夫
===
小人之依非知之難而行之難也商周盛王能
迪哲矣斯爲無逸之實與周公申之以勉成王
也意謂君人者孰不思爲小民計哉而率難善
治者凡以不知法古力行耳我思古人知民依
者有矣然知之而不能行猶弗知也矧曰其能
迪哲乎惟觀于殷有中宗高宗祖甲其人焉觀
于周有文王其人焉玆四人也本濬哲之神以
周悉乎民隱旣眞知而不遺推明哲之懿以善
體乎民情自允蹈而無歉治民祗懼中宗以之
punctuated:
以少愧矣。

自殷王中宗，及高宗，及祖甲，及我周文王，茲四人迪哲。
陳紹虞
同考試官訓導唐批：發揮「迪哲」二字，理精詞練，經義之最佳者，宜錄以式。
考試官訓導唐批：得周公告成王之旨。
考試官敎諭鄭批：明實。

大臣申言古人無逸之實，惟行其所知而已。夫小人之依，非知之難，而行之難也。商、周盛王能迪哲矣，斯爲無逸之實與！周公申之以勉成王也，意謂：君人者孰不思爲小民計哉？而率難善治者，凡以不知法古力行耳。我思古人知民依者有矣，然知之而不能行，猶弗知也，矧曰其能迪哲乎？惟觀于殷，有中宗、高宗、祖甲其人焉；觀于周，有文王其人焉。玆四人也，本濬哲之神，以周悉乎民隱，旣眞知而不遺；推明哲之懿，以善體乎民情，自允蹈而無歉。治民祗懼，中宗以之，
translation_en:
… feel somewhat ashamed!

"From King Zhongzong of Yin, to Gaozong, to Zujia, and to our King Wen of Zhou—these four men walked in wisdom."
Chen Shaoyu 陳紹虞
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Tang 唐 comments: In elaborating on the two words "walked in wisdom" (dizhe 迪哲), the reasoning is refined and the diction polished. It is the finest of the essays on the Classics and should be recorded as a model.
Examiner, Assistant Instructor Tang 唐 comments: It grasps the purport of the Duke of Zhou's admonition to King Cheng.
Examiner, Instructor Zheng 鄭 comments: Clear and substantial.

A great minister reiterates the reality of the ancients' refusal to indulge in ease: it lay simply in putting into practice what they knew. Now, as for what the common people depend upon, it is not knowing it that is difficult, but practicing it that is difficult. The flourishing kings of Shang and Zhou were able to walk in wisdom—was this not the very reality of refusing to indulge in ease! When the Duke of Zhou reiterated this to encourage King Cheng, his meaning was as follows: Who among those that rule over men does not think of planning for the common people? Yet the reason they generally find it difficult to achieve good governance is entirely because they do not know how to emulate antiquity and strive in practice. When I reflect upon the ancients, there were indeed those who knew what the people depended upon; yet to know it and be unable to practice it is the same as not knowing it at all—how much less could one say that they were able to walk in wisdom? Only when we look to Yin, there were such men as Zhongzong, Gaozong, and Zujia; and when we look to Zhou, there was such a man as King Wen. These four men grounded themselves in the spirit of profound wisdom so as to thoroughly comprehend the hidden sufferings of the people, truly knowing them without oversight; and they extended the excellence of their clear wisdom so as to sympathetically embody the conditions of the people, naturally fulfilling them in practice without deficiency. Governing the people with reverent trepidation—by this Zhongzong …

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
而高宗之嘉靖殷邦亦能蹈其知焉思其艱必
圖其易而實德之孚于民者合先後而其揆一
也保惠庶民祖甲以之而文王之咸和萬民亦
能踐其知焉知其依必奠其麗而實惠之及于
民者協異代而其道同也以小民艱難之狀為
九重獨見之猷而知之眞者又何嘗不行之至
乎商周之際所以惠養黎元者其在斯矣舉閭
閻疾苦之情為廟堂灼知之哲而察之精者又
何嘗不行之力乎二代之盛所以造福生靈者
===
其在茲矣夫惟其迪哲也是三宗文王所以永
也可為無逸者之法反是而不能迪哲也則非
所以紹前脩也寧不足為嗣王戒哉吁周公之
忠愛亦云至矣雖然成王亦令主也而無逸之
訓邠風之作周公所為惓惓而不置者豈過計
哉蓋周家以農事開國王業根本係焉周公欲
成王法祖為政甞懼其以逸心乘之故也厥後
成王果能繼美文王四三宗而稱哲王焉何莫
非周公之功哉
punctuated: 而高宗之嘉靖殷邦，亦能蹈其知焉。思其艱必圖其易，而實德之孚于民者，合先後而其揆一也。保惠庶民，祖甲以之，而文王之咸和萬民，亦能踐其知焉。知其依必奠其麗，而實惠之及于民者，協異代而其道同也。以小民艱難之狀，為九重獨見之猷，而知之眞者，又何嘗不行之至乎？商周之際，所以惠養黎元者，其在斯矣。舉閭閻疾苦之情，為廟堂灼知之哲，而察之精者，又何嘗不行之力乎？二代之盛，所以造福生靈者，其在茲矣。夫惟其迪哲也，是三宗、文王所以永也，可為無逸者之法；反是而不能迪哲也，則非所以紹前脩也，寧不足為嗣王戒哉！吁，周公之忠愛亦云至矣！雖然，成王亦令主也，而《無逸》之訓、《邠風》之作，周公所為惓惓而不置者，豈過計哉？蓋周家以農事開國，王業根本係焉，周公欲成王法祖為政，甞懼其以逸心乘之故也。厥後成王果能繼美文王，四三宗而稱哲王焉，何莫非周公之功哉！
translation_en: …and Gaozong's bringing peace and order to the state of Yin was likewise an instance of putting his knowledge into practice. Contemplating the hardships, they inevitably planned for what would bring ease, and the substantive virtue that inspired confidence in the people followed the same principle across earlier and later reigns. Protecting and showing kindness to the common people—this was how Zujia acted; and King Wen's harmonizing of all the myriad people was likewise an instance of fulfilling his knowledge in action. Knowing what the people depended upon, they inevitably secured their livelihood, and the substantive kindness that reached the people shared the same Way across different dynasties. Taking the hardships of the common folk as the personal counsels of the throne, how could those whose knowledge was genuine ever fail to carry it out to the utmost? In the eras of Shang and Zhou, the means by which the multitude were kindly nourished lay right here. Taking the sufferings of the village lanes as the clear-sighted wisdom of the court, how could those whose observation was penetrating ever fail to practice it with vigor? During the flourishing of the two dynasties, the means by which blessings were created for the living souls lay right here. Now, it was precisely because they walked in wisdom that the Three Ancestors and King Wen were able to enjoy long reigns, and they may serve as models for avoiding idleness; conversely, failing to walk in wisdom is no way to continue the achievements of worthy predecessors—how could this not suffice as a warning for successor kings! Alas, the loyalty and devotion of the Duke of Zhou may indeed be called supreme! Even so, King Cheng was also a fine ruler; why then did the Duke of Zhou remain so earnestly and unceasingly concerned in his instructions in "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) and his composition of the "Airs of Bin" (Binfeng)—was he being overly anxious? It was because the House of Zhou founded its state upon agriculture, on which the very root of the royal enterprise depended; desiring that King Cheng model his governance upon his ancestors, the Duke of Zhou was ever fearful lest a mind inclined to ease take hold of him. Thereafter, King Cheng was indeed able to carry on the admirable legacy of King Wen, standing as a fourth alongside the Three Ancestors to be acclaimed a wise king—how was any of this not owing to the merit of the Duke of Zhou!

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
詩
雝雝在宮肅肅在廟不顯亦臨無射亦保
歐陽勁
同考試官教諭梁批發揮文德之純詞簡意
盡可稱明經士矣
考試官訓導唐批詞瑩思徹邃養士也錄
以式
考試官教諭鄭批冲粹
詩人於聖君而極美其德之純焉甚矣文王之
===
德之純也肅雝交至而臨保常存茲文王之所
以為文歟此詠歌文王之德也意曰天下之稱
至德者惟其純焉止矣苟有一之未純非所以
語至德也文王之德其所自來遠矣而其德之
純也何如哉彼宮室之中其地親矣處親則道
貴和焉而文王之和非有所勉也徽柔之懿範
時溢于敦睦之餘在文王惟率其和親之則而
不自知其雝雝之至于于是者其和一何至耶宗
廟之內其地尊矣處尊則道貴敬焉而文王之
punctuated:
《詩》
「雝雝在宮，肅肅在廟。不顯亦臨，無射亦保。」
歐陽勁
同考試官教諭梁批：發揮文德之純，詞簡意盡，可稱明經士矣。
考試官訓導唐批：詞瑩思徹，邃養士也，錄以式。
考試官教諭鄭批：冲粹。
詩人於聖君，而極美其德之純焉。甚矣，文王之德之純也！肅雝交至，而臨保常存，茲文王之所以為文歟？此詠歌文王之德也，意曰：天下之稱至德者，惟其純焉止矣；苟有一之未純，非所以語至德也。文王之德，其所自來遠矣，而其德之純也何如哉？彼宮室之中，其地親矣，處親則道貴和焉，而文王之和，非有所勉也。徽柔之懿範，時溢于敦睦之餘，在文王惟率其和親之則，而不自知其雝雝之至于于是者，其和一何至耶！宗廟之內，其地尊矣，處尊則道貴敬焉，而文王之
translation_en:
Classic of Poetry (Shi)

"Harmonious, harmonious inside the palace; reverent, reverent inside the ancestral temple. Unseen, yet he feels overseen; untiring, he ever preserves it."

By Ouyang Jin 歐陽勁.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Liang 梁: It brings out the purity of King Wen's virtue; the diction is concise and the meaning is fully expressed. He may truly be called a scholar who understands the Classics.

Comment by Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang 唐: His words are pellucid and his thought penetrating; he is a scholar of deep cultivation. Recorded as a model.

Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zheng 鄭: Serene and pure.

With regard to the sage ruler, the poet praises the purity of his virtue to the utmost. How great indeed was the purity of King Wen's virtue! Reverence and harmony were both realized to perfection, and the sense of being overseen and of self-preservation abided constantly—was it not by this that King Wen came to be called "Wen" (Civil/Accomplished)?

These lines sing in praise of the virtue of King Wen. Their purport is as follows: What the world acclaims as supreme virtue stops at nothing other than its purity; if there is a single respect in which it is not pure, one cannot speak of it as supreme virtue. The virtue of King Wen had a remote origin indeed; and what was the purity of his virtue like?

There within the palace chambers, the place is one of intimacy; in dwelling amid intimacy, the Way prizes harmony—yet King Wen's harmony was not something forced. His admirable model of gentle mildness constantly overflowed in the course of fostering familial concord; as for King Wen, he simply followed the standard of harmonizing his kin without himself being conscious that his harmoniousness reached to such a degree [reading 于是 for 于于是]—how utterly complete was his harmony! Within the ancestral temple, the place is one of veneration; in dwelling amid veneration, the Way prizes reverence—yet King Wen's…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
敬非有所勉也懿恭之小心時嚴於對越之頃
在文王惟率其敬畏之衷而不自知其肅肅之
至于斯者其敬一何至耶至若人情每以顯而
臨以不顯而忽惟文王之視不顯猶顯也故雖
不睹不聞極天下之至幽而此心之翼翼者儼
乎上帝之臨矣當其時以聖心之敬止而猶不
忘夫緝熙者其以是哉人情每以射而保以無
射而弛惟文王之視無射猶射也故雖不思不
勉極天下之至善而此心之存存者兢乎持守
===
之密矣當其時以道岸之先登而猶望之若未
見者其以是哉是則在宮在廟異其地而聖心
之和敬不以地而間也不顯無射異其時而聖
心之敬畏不以時而間也文德之純一至于此
詩人詠歌之也其亦知德者乎抑吾於是而知
文王之心一天之心也天惟不已故天之化益
神聖德惟純故聖之脩益極天也文王也一而
已矣子思子言天之所以爲天又言文之所以
爲文而終之以純亦不已焉其旨深矣故曰觀
punctuated: 敬非有所勉也。懿恭之小心，時嚴於對越之頃。在文王惟率其敬畏之衷，而不自知其肅肅之至于斯者，其敬一何至耶！至若人情每以顯而臨，以不顯而忽，惟文王之視不顯猶顯也。故雖不睹不聞，極天下之至幽，而此心之翼翼者，儼乎上帝之臨矣。當其時，以聖心之敬止，而猶不忘夫緝熙者，其以是哉！人情每以射而保，以無射而弛，惟文王之視無射猶射也。故雖不思不勉，極天下之至善，而此心之存存者，兢乎持守之密矣。當其時，以道岸之先登，而猶望之若未見者，其以是哉！是則在宮在廟異其地，而聖心之和敬不以地而間也；不顯無射異其時，而聖心之敬畏不以時而間也。文德之純一至于此，詩人詠歌之也，其亦知德者乎！抑吾於是而知文王之心，一天之心也。天惟不已，故天之化益神；聖德惟純，故聖之脩益極。天也，文王也，一而已矣。子思子言天之所以爲天，又言文之所以爲文，而終之以「純亦不已」焉，其旨深矣。故曰：觀
translation_en: …reverence was not something forced. His admirable, respectful mindfulness was ever strict in the moments of standing before the spirits. For King Wen simply followed his inner feelings of reverence and awe, without being conscious himself that his solemnity reached such a point—how utterly extreme was his reverence! As for human nature, people always act as though watched when in the open, yet grow negligent when unseen; only King Wen regarded the unseen just as he did the manifest. Thus, even in what is neither seen nor heard—the utmost obscurity in the world—the cautious vigilance of his mind was as solemn as if the Lord on High were descending before him. At that time, though his sage mind already rested in reverence, he still did not forget continuous illumination—was it not because of this? Human nature always strives to preserve when weary of failing, yet relaxes when free of weariness; only King Wen regarded being unweary just as he did being prone to weariness. Thus, even in hitting the mark without thought or effort—the utmost perfection in the world—the ceaseless preservation of his mind remained apprehension-filled in the rigor of its self-possession. At that time, though he had already ascended the shore of the Way, he still looked toward it as though he had not yet seen it—was it not because of this? Thus, being in the palace and being in the ancestral temple differ in place, yet the harmony and reverence of the sage's mind are not interrupted by place; being unseen and being unweary differ in time, yet the reverence and awe of the sage's mind are not interrupted by time. That the purity and unity of King Wen's virtue reached such a height—when the poet sang of it, was he not indeed one who understood virtue? Moveover, from this I know that the mind of King Wen is one with the mind of Heaven. Only because Heaven is ceaseless do Heaven's transformations become all the more wondrous; only because the sage's virtue is pure does the sage's self-cultivation reach the utmost extreme. Heaven and King Wen are simply one. Master Zisi spoke of that by which Heaven is Heaven, and spoke again of that by which King Wen was called "Cultured" (Wen), concluding with "its purity likewise never ceases"—his meaning is profound indeed. Therefore it is said: By observing…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
天則知聖人
四海來假來假祁祁景員維河殷受命咸
宜百祿是何
黃淳
同考試官教諭楊批發商家世業世德之盛
詳盡簡古宜錄以式
考試官訓導唐批精確
考試官教諭鄭批警健
商人申言賢王一統之業而推其世德之得天
===
也夫業隆一統則受天命而何百祿矣而惟世
德以宜之此賢王所以爲天下烈歟宜商人歌
於廟祀以揚其盛也蓋謂一代王業之興豈偶
然哉必有盛德者爲之前焉尤必有盛德者爲
之後焉惟德盛而後其業隆也吾觀武丁而知
商之德與商之所以王也已何則王假有廟萃
人心也乃今龍旂建矣大禧承矣四海之康侯
悉萃焉假廟之人文矣何異于方命之初乎皇
建有極大一統也乃今邦畿奠矣肇域廣矣景
punctuated:
天，則知聖人。

「四海來假，來假祁祁，景員維河。殷受命咸宜，百祿是何。」
黃淳
同考試官、教諭楊批：發商家世業世德之盛，詳盡簡古，宜錄以式。
考試官、訓導唐批：精確。
考試官、教諭鄭批：警健。

商人申言賢王一統之業，而推其世德之得天也。夫業隆一統，則受天命而何百祿矣；而惟世德以宜之，此賢王所以爲天下烈歟！宜商人歌於廟祀，以揚其盛也。蓋謂一代王業之興，豈偶然哉？必有盛德者爲之前焉，尤必有盛德者爲之後焉；惟德盛而後其業隆也。吾觀武丁，而知商之德與商之所以王也已。何則？王假有廟，萃人心也。乃今龍旂建矣，大禧承矣，四海之康侯悉萃焉，假廟之人文矣，何異于方命之初乎？皇建有極，大一統也。乃今邦畿奠矣，肇域廣矣，景
translation_en:
… Heaven, one understands the Sage.

"Those from within the four seas come in homage; they come in homage in great multitudes; the grand borders are bounded by the Yellow River. That Yin receives the Mandate is wholly fitting, and a hundred blessings it bears."
Huang Chun 黃淳
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Yang 楊: It brings out the flourishing of the royal house of Shang's hereditary enterprise and hereditary virtue; thorough, concise, and classic in style—it should be recorded as a model.
Comment by Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang 唐: Precise and exact.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zheng 鄭: Incisive and vigorous.

The people of Shang reiterate the unifying enterprise of their worthy king, and trace it to how their hereditary virtue won the favor of Heaven. Now, when an enterprise reaches the height of grand unification, one receives the Mandate of Heaven and bears a hundred blessings; yet it is only through hereditary virtue that one is worthy of it—is this not how the worthy king achieved supreme merit across the realm! Fittingly did the people of Shang sing of this at the ancestral temple sacrifices to extol its magnificence. For how could the rise of a dynasty's royal enterprise be mere coincidence? There must first be one of abundant virtue who precedes it, and even more must there be one of abundant virtue who succeeds it; only when virtue is abundant does the enterprise flourish. Observing Wu Ding 武丁, I know the virtue of Shang and the reason why Shang ruled as true kings. Why is this so? When the king approaches the ancestral temple, he gathers together the hearts of the people. Now the dragon-banners have been raised, the great sacrificial grain has been presented, and the peaceful lords of the four seas have all gathered here in homage, forming the splendid assembly of those approaching the temple—how does this differ from the very beginning when the Mandate was first received? When the sovereign establishes the supreme standard, he achieves a grand unification. Now the royal domain is securely settled, the bounded territory is vast, and the…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
河之形勝悉屬于有商之幅員矣何改于奄有
之舊乎是人心也土宇也皆君之祿也皆天之
命也而非德則無以宜之也維昔有成湯而德
以基命者已何天祿於其前維今有武丁而德
以保命者又何天祿於其後有人之命以一德
而昭受之宜也非幸也人心之攸同即諸福之
畢集視諸何天休而遒百祿者其媲隆也已有
土之命以一德而寵受之宜也非幸也土宇之
皈章即繁祉之駢臻視諸何天寵而總百祿者
===
其濟美也已由是而知我商之業有湯以為之
前美而彰矣有武丁以為之後盛而傳矣此守
成之賢有光于創業而頌成湯之烈者固宜稱
武丁之功不衰歟抑武丁何脩而得此哉蓋本
之以恭默思道之學而成之以鹽梅舟楫之助
人巳夾持世德克懋此商道之所以赫然興也
商人祭祀而惓惓以祖德為言無亦以法祖望
其君歟撫成業者尚繹思之
春秋
punctuated:
河之形勝，悉屬于有商之幅員矣，何改于奄有之舊乎？是人心也，土宇也，皆君之祿也，皆天之命也，而非德則無以宜之也。維昔有成湯，而德以基命者，已何天祿於其前；維今有武丁，而德以保命者，又何天祿於其後。有人之命，以一德而昭受之，宜也，非幸也；人心之攸同，即諸福之畢集，視諸何天休而遒百祿者，其媲隆也已。有土之命，以一德而寵受之，宜也，非幸也；土宇之皈章，即繁祉之駢臻，視諸何天寵而總百祿者，其濟美也已。由是而知我商之業，有湯以為之前，美而彰矣；有武丁以為之後，盛而傳矣。此守成之賢，有光于創業，而頌成湯之烈者，固宜稱武丁之功不衰歟！抑武丁何脩而得此哉？蓋本之以恭默思道之學，而成之以鹽梅舟楫之助，人巳夾持，世德克懋，此商道之所以赫然興也。商人祭祀，而惓惓以祖德為言，無亦以法祖望其君歟？撫成業者，尚繹思之。

《春秋》
translation_en:
…and the strategic topography of Mount Jing and the Yellow River all belong within the territorial bounds of the Shang—how has it changed at all from the old days when the realm was first encompassed? Both these hearts of the people and these territories are the blessings of the ruler and the Mandate of Heaven, yet without virtue there is no way to be worthy of them. In the past there was Cheng Tang, who through virtue established the Mandate and already bore the blessings of Heaven before; now there is Wu Ding, who through virtue preserves the Mandate and again bears the blessings of Heaven after. That the mandate to possess the people was gloriously received through pure and constant virtue was fitting, not mere fortune; the unison of the people's hearts is itself the complete gathering of all blessings, and compared to him who bore Heaven's favor and brought together the hundred blessings, it is equally magnificent! That the mandate to possess the territory was graciously received through pure and constant virtue was fitting, not mere fortune; the vastness of the domain is itself the arrival of abundant felicities side by side, and compared to him who bore Heaven's grace and gathered all the hundred blessings, it carries forward the same splendor! From this we know that the enterprise of our Shang, having Tang to go before, became admirable and illustrious; and having Wu Ding to follow after, became flourishing and enduring. Thus the worthiness of one who preserves an accomplished enterprise adds luster to the founding of it, and those who eulogize the illustrious achievements of Cheng Tang ought indeed to praise the unfailing merits of Wu Ding! Yet what cultivation did Wu Ding practice to attain this? It was rooted in the learning of reverent silence and contemplation of the Way, and brought to completion by the assistance of ministers who served like salt and plum for seasoning or boats and oars for crossing waters. With others and oneself mutually supporting one another, the hereditary virtue was richly cultivated, and this is how the Way of Shang revived so gloriously. When the people of Shang performed their sacrifices and spoke so earnestly of ancestral virtue, was it not also out of hope that their ruler would model himself upon his ancestors? Let those who hold custody of an established enterprise ponder this deeply.

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
衞人救陳〔宣公十有二年〕會于蕭魚〔襄公〕
〔十有一年〕
梁尚通
同考試官學正趙批〔體傳精詳措詞秀雅可〕
〔錄〕
考試官訓導唐批〔措詞婉轉用事精贍藝〕
〔林匠手也〕
考試官敎諭鄭批〔嚴整〕
春秋紀受過讓善之事所以敎天下忠也此孔
達之過任於已魏絳之善歸於君皆忠道也春
秋取之其亦以愧澶平者與華元子反結成而
二國平焉人方以一時之功壯之矣曰獨不聞
有孔達之任過者乎方宋之討陳而衞之救之
也晉致渝盟之討人孰不避罪而退者達則思
執政自已於君何尤也乃曰請以我說焉危能
授命式昭任事之勇難無苟免不爲全軀之謀
雖其伉伯奸宋而先君之諾是踐固亦謀之不
臧者然不論其謀國之非而惟取其慷慨之義
punctuated:

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the affairs of accepting blame and yielding credit for goodness in order to teach loyalty to all under Heaven. That Kong Da 孔達 took the fault upon himself and Wei Jiang 魏絳 attributed the goodness to his ruler are both the way of loyalty. In approving of them, did the Spring and Autumn Annals not also intend to put to shame those who made peace at Chan [or: those who gloried in a private peace]? When Hua Yuan 華元 and Zifan 子反 concluded a settlement and the two states made peace, people at the time praised them for the achievement of the moment. Yet one asked: "Have you alone not heard of Kong Da, who took the blame upon himself?" Just when Song was punishing Chen and Wei rescued it, Jin pressed its chastisement for violating the covenant. Who among men would not have shirked the guilt and retreated? Da, however, reflected that the administration of state affairs had proceeded from himself—what fault was it of his ruler's? Thus he said: "Please use me to explain this away." In peril he was able to offer up his life, thereby manifesting the courage of one who takes responsibility for affairs; in crisis he refused to逃escape ignobly, making no plans to preserve his own person. Although in defying the hegemon and offending Song to fulfill the promise of his former ruler, his counsel was admittedly not good, nevertheless, if we disregard the error of his statecraft and solely approve his heroic righteousness, …

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
則亦庶幾哉國爾忘家君爾忘身之忠也已又
不聞有魏絳之讓善者乎方晉之服鄭而鄭之
饋樂也君致和戎之賞人孰不貪功焉力者絳
則思諸侯賓服實君之靈也乃曰臣何力焉勞
而能謙持成功于不宰滿而知損讓大美于一
人雖其以夏交戎而内外之防以潰固亦策之
無良者然不論其建策之失而惟取其卑遜之
節則亦庶幾哉有功不伐有能不矜之忠也已
彼元反者取必於已以成平國之功而君不與
===
焉是以息兵之善歸已而以構怨之過歸君也
即使過非孔達孰若以達之處過處之善同魏
絳孰若以絳之讓善讓之哉雖然君子尚有遺
論焉華元素多大勳國人所與視之三駕之功
絳有成勞者何異元與絳均之晉宋之良也已
彼孔達賈禍身不償責與子反相楚助桀為虐
又安有軒輊也尚論者當合而觀之
冬鄭公孫夏帥師伐陳襄公二十有五年
劉堯佐
punctuated:
則亦庶幾哉，國爾忘家、君爾忘身之忠也已。又不聞有魏絳之讓善者乎？方晉之服鄭而鄭之饋樂也，君致和戎之賞，人孰不貪功焉力者？絳則思諸侯賓服，實君之靈也，乃曰：「臣何力焉？」勞而能謙，持成功于不宰；滿而知損，讓大美于一人。雖其以夏交戎，而内外之防以潰，固亦策之無良者；然不論其建策之失，而惟取其卑遜之節，則亦庶幾哉，有功不伐、有能不矜之忠也已。彼元、反者，取必於已，以成平國之功，而君不與焉，是以息兵之善歸已，而以構怨之過歸君也。即使過非孔達，孰若以達之處過處之？善同魏絳，孰若以絳之讓善讓之哉？雖然，君子尚有遺論焉。華元素多大勳，國人所與，視之三駕之功、絳有成勞者何異？元與絳，均之晉、宋之良也已。彼孔達賈禍，身不償責，與子反相楚、助桀為虐，又安有軒輊也？尚論者當合而觀之。
冬，鄭公孫夏帥師伐陳。襄公二十有五年。
劉堯佐
translation_en:
…then this too comes close to the loyalty of forgetting one's family for the sake of the state and forgetting one's own person for the sake of the ruler! And have they not heard of Wei Jiang's 魏絳 yielding of credit for a good deed? Just when Jin had brought Zheng to submission and Zheng presented a gift of musical instruments, the ruler bestowed rewards on him for making peace with the Rong; who would not have been greedy for the merit as his own achievement [?]? Yet Jiang reflected that the submission of the feudal lords was truly due to the prestige of his ruler, and so he said: "What effort of your servant was there in this?" Having toiled, he was able to be modest, holding onto accomplished merit without claiming mastery over it; when full, he knew how to diminish himself, yielding the great credit to the One Man. Although in having the Chinese states enter into relations with the Rong he caused the barrier between the inner and the outer to be breached—which was indeed an unsound policy—yet if one sets aside the error of his proposed policy and takes only his humble and yielding integrity, then this too comes close to the loyalty of having merit without boasting and having ability without bragging!

As for those two, Hua Yuan and Zifan, they insisted on deciding matters themselves to accomplish the merit of making peace between the states, without their rulers taking part in it; thus they attributed the goodness of halting hostilities to themselves, while attributing the fault of incurring enmity to their rulers. Even if their fault was not like that of Kong Da, how could their conduct compare with dealing with fault the way Da dealt with his fault? And even if their good achievement was similar to that of Wei Jiang, how could it compare with yielding credit the way Jiang yielded his credit?

Even so, the gentleman still has a further judgment to make. Hua Yuan had always possessed great and numerous merits and enjoyed the support of the people of his state; how did he differ from Jiang, who had accomplished service in the merit of the Three Expeditions? Both Yuan and Jiang were alike worthy ministers of Jin and Song. As for that Kong Da, who courted disaster so that his own death could not atone for his responsibility, and Zifan, who served as minister of Chu and aided a tyrant in doing evil—what difference in merit is there between them? Those who evaluate the men of antiquity ought to consider them together.

"In winter, Gongsun Xia 公孫夏 of Zheng led a force to attack Chen" (25th year of Duke Xiang 襄公).
By Liu Yaozuo 劉堯佐.

translation_en:
… then this too comes close to the loyalty of "for the state, forgetting one's family; for the ruler, forgetting one's own person"! And have you not heard of Wei Jiang's yielding of credit for a good deed? Just when Jin had subjugated Zheng and Zheng presented musical instruments, the ruler bestowed upon him the reward for making peace with the Rong; who among men would not covet the merit and claim the effort as his own? Yet Jiang reflected that the submission of the feudal lords was truly due to the ruler's numinous authority, and thus said, "What effort of your servant was there in this?" Having toiled yet able to be humble, he held onto accomplished merit without claiming mastery over it; at fullness yet knowing how to diminish himself, he yielded great excellence to the One Man [his ruler]. Although his associating the Xia [Chinese states] with the Rong caused the barrier between inner and outer to collapse, which was admittedly an unsound policy, if we set aside the flaw in his policy proposal and take only his integrity in humble deference, then this too comes close to the loyalty of "having merit without boasting, having ability without bragging"! As for those two, [Hua] Yuan and [Zi]fan, they insisted on acting on their own authority to accomplish the merit of making peace between their states, without their rulers taking part in it; this was to attribute the goodness of halting hostilities to themselves, while attributing the fault of incurring enmity to their rulers. Even if their fault was not like that of Kong Da, how could their conduct compare to handling a fault the way Da handled his? And even if their good deed was like that of Wei Jiang, how could it compare to yielding credit for a good deed the way Jiang yielded his? Even so, the gentleman still has a further observation to make. Hua Yuan always had great and numerous achievements and enjoyed the support of the people of the state; compared with the merit of the Three Expeditions, in which Jiang had established toil, what difference was there? Yuan and Jiang were alike worthy ministers of Jin and Song. As for Kong Da, who courted disaster and whose death could not atone for his responsibility, and Zifan, who assisted Chu like helping Jie perpetrate tyranny—how could one be ranked above or below the other? Those who evaluate the figures of antiquity ought to consider all of these aspects together.

"In winter, Gongsun Xia of Zheng led a force to attack Chen" (25th year of Duke Xiang)
By Liu Yaozuo

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
拜孫夏復伐必得其平而晉卒不能有加于鄭
以謂鄭之能抗晉也如此而不知以僑之能馳
詞也謂晉之有畏于鄭也如此而不知以僑之
能執禮也不然晉國天下莫強焉將悉鄭之力
有不能得志者而竟得之一介使哉夫昭盟府
之勳者解懸磬之恥伸德義之辨者遏鼓躁之
威彼聖人之化尚矣而僑將不得爲展禽哉然
則鄭忽以世嫡之胄國君之貴乃不自立而受
制於人其視子產爲何如吾於是知得人則理
===
失人則亂理之必不可誣者坎坎伐檀置之河
干固非國家之利毋金玉爾音而有遐心人君
寤寐英豪當如此
禮記
君命大夫與士肄在官言官在府言府在
庫言庫在朝言朝
蒙而鉉
同考試官教諭侯批沖淡中有雅趣平正中
吐竒葩肄君命意作者非冗則疎子獨發之瑩然
punctuated:
拜，孫夏復伐，必得其平，而晉卒不能有加于鄭。以謂鄭之能抗晉也如此，而不知以僑之能馳詞也；謂晉之有畏于鄭也如此，而不知以僑之能執禮也。不然，晉國天下莫強焉，將悉鄭之力有不能得志者，而竟得之一介使哉？夫昭盟府之勳者，解懸磬之恥；伸德義之辨者，遏鼓躁之威。彼聖人之化尚矣，而僑將不得爲展禽哉？然則鄭忽以世嫡之胄、國君之貴，乃不自立而受制於人，其視子產爲何如？吾於是知得人則理、失人則亂，理之必不可誣者。「坎坎伐檀，置之河干」，固非國家之利；「毋金玉爾音，而有遐心」，人君寤寐英豪，當如此。

translation_en:
…accepted with a bow; and when Gongsun Xia 公孫夏 attacked once more, Zheng made sure to secure peace terms from Chen, while Jin was ultimately unable to impose anything further upon Zheng. One might say that this showed how capable Zheng was of resisting Jin, without realizing that it was because of Gongsun Qiao's 公孫僑 (Zichan 子產) skill in presenting diplomatic arguments; one might say that this showed how wary Jin was of Zheng, without realizing that it was because of Qiao's ability to uphold ritual propriety. Otherwise, since no state in the world was stronger than Jin, how could an outcome that Zheng could not have achieved even by exhausting all its military strength ultimately be won by a single envoy? Indeed, he who made manifest the meritorious records in the archives of covenants relieved the humiliation of a state as depleted as a hanging musical stone, and he who set forth the distinction between virtue and righteousness checked the bluster of clamoring troops. The transforming influence of the sages is of course supreme, yet could Qiao not at least be counted another Zhan Qin 展禽 (Liuxia Hui 柳下惠)? If so, then when Zheng Hu 鄭忽, despite his lineage as the legitimate eldest heir and his exalted station as ruler of a state, failed to stand on his own and instead allowed himself to be controlled by others, how does he compare with Zichan? From this I know that obtaining worthy men brings order and losing them brings disorder—a principle that can never be falsified. "Chop, chop they cut the sandalwood, and leave it on the river's bank"—this is surely not to the advantage of the state; "Do not treat your voice like gold and jade, or harbor a distant heart"—thus should a ruler long waking and sleeping for heroic talents.

Record of Rites (Liji)
"When the ruler issues a command, the Grand Masters and Servitors rehearse it: in the offices they speak of office business, in the treasuries they speak of treasury business, in the armories they speak of armory business, and at court they speak of court business."
By Meng Erxuan 蒙而鉉
Associate Examiner and Instructor Hou comments: "Within its tranquil simplicity there is refined grace; out of its balanced directness blossom rare flowers. On the meaning of rehearsing the ruler's commands, other writers are either verbose or sketchy; you alone have elucidated it with crystal clarity, …"

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
非有體認實學不能到
考試官訓導唐批〔精貫無遺〕
考試官敎諭鄭批〔融徹〕
人臣之習君命也隨事而異其言焉夫官府庫
朝事不同也而言亦因之以異焉其殆善於習
君命者乎且君制命焉臣致君之命以布諸民
焉君臣之交其相待以有成也久矣故君命有
頒所以統治權也爲大夫士者分雖間於尊卑
之殊而心實同夫奉若之忱命之斯肄之矣肄
===
當何如官也府也庫也朝也均之關於政而爲
王命之所必及者也則言官也言府也言庫也
言朝也均之承王命而爲臣職之不容怠者也
故命降於官則所言者官而不得以府雜之至
于言府亦當其在府斯言之耳而胡敢二三其
習也命降於庫則所言者庫而不得以朝雜之
至于言朝亦當其在朝斯言之耳而胡敢肄之
不專也大夫總其綱焉官府庫朝不一其事而
亦不一其言蓋君命所在吾惟知專此心以肄
punctuated:
非有體認實學不能到。
考試官訓導唐批：〔精貫無遺。〕
考試官敎諭鄭批：〔融徹。〕
人臣之習君命也，隨事而異其言焉。夫官、府、庫、朝，事不同也，而言亦因之以異焉，其殆善於習君命者乎！且君制命焉，臣致君之命以布諸民焉，君臣之交，其相待以有成也久矣。故君命有頒，所以統治權也；爲大夫、士者，分雖間於尊卑之殊，而心實同夫奉若之忱。命之斯肄之矣，肄當何如？官也、府也、庫也、朝也，均之關於政，而爲王命之所必及者也；則言官也、言府也、言庫也、言朝也，均之承王命，而爲臣職之不容怠者也。故命降於官，則所言者官，而不得以府雜之；至于言府，亦當其在府斯言之耳，而胡敢二三其習也！命降於庫，則所言者庫，而不得以朝雜之；至于言朝，亦當其在朝斯言之耳，而胡敢肄之不專也！大夫總其綱焉，官、府、庫、朝不一其事，而亦不一其言，蓋君命所在，吾惟知專此心以肄

…Without personally experienced, substantial learning, one could not have attained this.
Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang 唐 commented: [Thoroughly coherent, leaving nothing out.]
Examiner and Instructor Zheng 鄭 commented: [Harmoniously penetrating.]
When a subject practices the ruler's commands, he varies his words according to the affair. Now the government office, the treasury of documents, the storehouse, and the court involve different affairs, and one's words accordingly vary with them; is this not indeed to be skilled at practicing the ruler's commands! Moreover, the ruler formulates commands, and the subjects convey the ruler's commands to promulgate them among the people; in the interaction between ruler and subject, their mutual dependence to achieve success has long been the case. Therefore, when the ruler's commands are issued, it is the means by which governing authority is unified; as for those who are grand masters and servicemen, although their stations are separated by the distinction between noble and humble, their minds are truly identical in the sincerity of their reverent compliance. Once commanded, they practice it; how then should they practice it? The government office, the treasury of documents, the storehouse, and the court all alike pertain to governance and are places that the royal commands must reach; thus speaking of the government office, speaking of the treasury of documents, speaking of the storehouse, and speaking of the court all alike involve receiving the royal commands and are ministerial duties in which negligence cannot be tolerated. Therefore, when a command comes down concerning the government office, what is spoken of is the government office, and one must not mix matters of the treasury of documents into it; as for speaking of the treasury of documents, it is also only when one is in the treasury of documents that one speaks of it—how would one dare to be divided in one's practice! When a command comes down concerning the storehouse, what is spoken of is the storehouse, and one must not mix matters of the court into it; as for speaking of the court, it is also only when one is at court that one speaks of it—how would one dare to be unfocused in one's practice! The grand masters oversee the general outlines: in the government office, the treasury of documents, the storehouse, and the court, the affairs are not uniform, and the words are likewise not uniform; for wherever the ruler's command lies, I know only to concentrate this mind in order to practice…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
本之不立而足以基化化之未行而足以象德
者也君子旣廣樂之方以敎民矣及夫太和洋
溢而遵道者效則君之治至順流通而嚮風者
有從欲之休樂行於平情而民之情因以正焉
養其善心滌其邪穢曉然不迷於至善之途也
樂行於道志而民之志因以和焉以之好善以
之聽過昭然不惑於向道之域也如是而君子
之盛德不可觀乎吾知德在君而未始不通諸
民化在民而未始不本諸君也故卽民習之丕
===
變可以驗其養盛之休因民則之式和可以探
其純粹之蘊情之正矣雖人人而具之然治之
隆者積之厚也化溥天下機本吾身君子情正
之德至此無以加矣志之和矣雖盡人而有之
然俗之美者養之隆也道徵諸人機先乎已君
子志和之德至此無以尚矣樂非彰德之至要
者哉信乎必積中而後可以發外有天德乃可
以語王道也君子旣知其化之盛而又知其德
之神則所以端化本者不容已矣大抵廣其節
punctuated: 本之不立，而足以基化；化之未行，而足以象德者也。君子旣廣樂之方以敎民矣，及夫太和洋溢，而遵道者效，則君之治至順流通，而嚮風者有從欲之休。樂行於平情，而民之情因以正焉，養其善心，滌其邪穢，曉然不迷於至善之途也；樂行於道志，而民之志因以和焉，以之好善，以之聽過，昭然不惑於向道之域也。如是而君子之盛德不可觀乎？吾知德在君而未始不通諸民，化在民而未始不本諸君也。故卽民習之丕變，可以驗其養盛之休；因民則之式和，可以探其純粹之蘊。情之正矣，雖人人而具之，然治之隆者積之厚也，化溥天下，機本吾身，君子情正之德至此無以加矣；志之和矣，雖盡人而有之，然俗之美者養之隆也，道徵諸人，機先乎已，君子志和之德至此無以尚矣。樂非彰德之至要者哉！信乎必積中而後可以發外，有天德乃可以語王道也。君子旣知其化之盛，而又知其德之神，則所以端化本者不容已矣。大抵廣其節
translation_en: …[never has there been a case where] the root is not established and yet it suffices to lay the foundation for transformation, or where transformation has not yet taken effect and yet it suffices to symbolize virtue. Once the noble man has broadened the methods of music in order to instruct the people, when supreme harmony brims over and those who follow the Way emulate it, the ruler's governance flows with utmost smoothness, and those who turn toward his influence enjoy the blessing of following their proper desires. When music operates by pacifying the emotions, the people's emotions are thereby rectified—nurturing their good hearts and washing away their perverse impurities, so that they clearly do not lose their way on the path to supreme goodness. When music operates by guiding the will, the people's wills are thereby harmonized—using it to love goodness and using it to heed their faults, so that they brightly avoid confusion in the realm of turning toward the Way. When it is like this, can the flourishing virtue of the noble man not be observed? I know that while virtue resides in the ruler, it never fails to communicate itself to the people; and while transformation resides in the people, it never fails to be rooted in the ruler. Therefore, from the great transformation of the people's habits, one can verify the beauty of his flourishing self-cultivation; through the harmonious modeling of the people's norms, one can fathom the depths of his pure essence. Once the emotions are rectified, although every person possesses this rectitude, the grandeur of governance comes from the thickness of accumulation: transformation spreads throughout the world, yet its pivot is rooted in one's own person, and the noble man's virtue of rectified emotions can have nothing added to it at this point. Once the will is harmonized, although all people have this harmony, the beauty of customs comes from the richness of nourishment: the Way is attested in others, yet its pivot begins in oneself, and the noble man's virtue of a harmonized will cannot be surpassed at this point. Is music not the most essential means of manifesting virtue? Truly, one must accumulate within before one can issue forth without, and only when one possesses heavenly virtue can one speak of the Kingly Way. Since the noble man knows the flourishing of his transformation and also knows the marvelousness of his virtue, his efforts to make upright the root of transformation cannot cease. In general, broadening its rhythms…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
奏樂之末也省其文采德之餘也君子審一以
定和然後比物以飾節夫是以心和氣和而天
下之和應不然徒求之聲音舞蹈而曰可以感
人心而天下和平豈理也哉
第貳場
論
周家王業根本
黃淳
同考試官教諭李批筆力雄渾發重本之意
===
精切末復歸重守成擇相意尤得肯綮此必邃養
者錄之以式多士
考試官訓導唐批爽勁脫塵
考試官教諭鄭批簡古
古之聖王所以立萬世之基者其本於立民之
命乎夫王者之所天在民民之所天在稼穡稼
穡不務則重違其所天而民命不立民命不立
則邦本不固如天下何如國家不拔之基業何
明主辨之蚤矣故他務未遑惓惓焉惟農桑是
punctuated:
奏，樂之末也；省其文采，德之餘也。君子審一以定和，然後比物以飾節，夫是以心和氣和而天下之和應。不然，徒求之聲音舞蹈，而曰可以感人心而天下和平，豈理也哉！
第貳場
論
周家王業根本
黃淳
同考試官教諭李批：筆力雄渾，發重本之意精切；末復歸重守成擇相，意尤得肯綮。此必邃養者，錄之以式多士。
考試官訓導唐批：爽勁脫塵。
考試官教諭鄭批：簡古。
古之聖王所以立萬世之基者，其本於立民之命乎！夫王者之所天在民，民之所天在稼穡。稼穡不務，則重違其所天，而民命不立；民命不立，則邦本不固，如天下何？如國家不拔之基業何？明主辨之蚤矣，故他務未遑，惓惓焉惟農桑是
translation_en:
…and rhythms is merely the secondary aspect of music; examining its ornamental patterns is merely the surplus of virtue. The gentleman investigates the one fundamental principle in order to establish harmony, and only afterward coordinates the musical instruments in order to refine the rhythm. Thus, his mind is harmonious, his vital energy is harmonious, and the harmony of the world responds to him. Otherwise, if one merely seeks it in sounds, tones, and dances, while claiming that this can move people's hearts and bring peace to the world—how could that be reasonable?

Second Session
Discourse
"The Fundamental Basis of the Royal Enterprise of the House of Zhou"
Huang Chun 黃淳
Associate Examiner and Instructor Li 李 comments: The brushwork is vigorous and profound, expressing the meaning of emphasizing the fundamental with precision and incisiveness. At the end, it returns to emphasizing the preservation of achievements and the selection of chief ministers, an idea that especially hits the crucial point. This must be a person of deep cultivation; we record it to serve as a model for the many scholars.
Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang 唐 comments: Brisk, forceful, and transcendent.
Examiner and Instructor Zheng 鄭 comments: Concise and古-style (antiquarian/classic).

That by which the sage kings of antiquity established a foundation for ten thousand generations—was it not rooted in establishing the livelihood of the people? Now, what the true king regards as Heaven is the people, and what the people regard as Heaven is sowing and reaping. If sowing and reaping are not attended to, then one gravely violates what they regard as Heaven, and the livelihood of the people is not established. If the livelihood of the people is not established, then the foundation of the state is not secure—what then can be done for the realm? What then can be done for the unshakeable foundational enterprise of the state? Enlightened rulers discerned this early on; therefore, before having leisure for other affairs, they earnestly and solely attended to agriculture and sericulture…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之制禮作樂識泰平之天子外之越裳西旅歌
中國之聖人則又根深而發榮本固而末茂而
王業其益盛矣何也王者以民爲本民以衣食
爲本而農桑又爲衣食之本重農桑是卽重民
之本而重民之本乃所以培王業之根本也彼
德之隆也功之偉也治之巍然赫然也何者而
不根本於是哉有周王業之興邁夏商而追勳
華良非偶矣抑嘗合而觀之周家王業根本其
樹立開先固后稷以來之功而栽培滋養使太
===
和在成周宇宙間彌久而彌固者則成王守成
之力居多也夫創業之主發跡壠畝其於小民
之依□□知之無難繼體之君足不越巖廊
目未嘗表畒庸知農桑爲何物耶自非神明特
達付託得人則八珍在前九嬪在御四方六合
之衆吾得臣妾而頤指氣使之則上之窮蓬萊
煉金石而疲天下以必不可致之事次之標銅
柱走天馬竭百姓力爭不必有之土而臣必不
可臣之民下之則馳逐三風弁髦億兆窮奢極
punctuated: 之制禮作樂，識泰平之天子；外之越裳、西旅，歌中國之聖人。則又根深而發榮，本固而末茂，而王業其益盛矣！何也？王者以民爲本，民以衣食爲本，而農桑又爲衣食之本。重農桑是卽重民之本，而重民之本乃所以培王業之根本也。彼德之隆也，功之偉也，治之巍然赫然也，何者而不根本於是哉？有周王業之興，邁夏、商而追勳華，良非偶矣。抑嘗合而觀之，周家王業根本，其樹立開先，固后稷以來之功；而栽培滋養，使太和在成周宇宙間，彌久而彌固者，則成王守成之力居多也。夫創業之主，發跡壠畝，其於小民之依，□□知之無難。繼體之君，足不越巖廊，目未嘗表畒，庸知農桑爲何物耶？自非神明特達，付託得人，則八珍在前，九嬪在御，四方六合之衆，吾得臣妾而頤指氣使之。則上之窮蓬萊、煉金石，而疲天下以必不可致之事；次之標銅柱、走天馬，竭百姓力，爭不必有之土，而臣必不可臣之民；下之則馳逐三風，弁髦億兆，窮奢極
translation_en: …within the realm, instituting rites and creating music, they recognized a Son of Heaven of great peace; beyond the realm, the Yuechang and the Western Lü sang praises of the Sage in the Central States. Thus the roots were deep and the blossoms flourished, the foundation was firm and the branches were luxuriant, and the royal enterprise grew ever more prosperous! Why was this so? Because a true king takes the people as his foundation, the people take food and clothing as their foundation, and agriculture and sericulture are in turn the foundation of food and clothing. To value agriculture and sericulture is thus to value the foundation of the people, and valuing the foundation of the people is the means by which one nurtures the root and foundation of the royal enterprise. That lofty virtue, those magnificent achievements, and that towering, illustrious governance—which of them was not rooted in this? That the rise of the royal enterprise of the Zhou surpassed the Xia and Shang and rivaled Yao and Shun was truly no accident. Yet if we consider the whole picture together, as for the root and foundation of the royal enterprise of the House of Zhou, its establishment and pioneering were indeed the achievement of Hou Ji and his successors; whereas its cultivation and nourishment, causing supreme harmony to abide throughout the universe of the Zhou at its height, becoming ever firmer with the passage of time, was largely due to King Cheng's efforts in preserving what had been achieved. Now, the founder of a dynasty rises from the fields and ridges; as for the livelihood upon which the common people depend, [he has personally experienced it and [?]] has no difficulty knowing it. A succeeding ruler, however, never sets foot beyond the lofty halls of the court and his eyes have never seen the boundary markers of the fields—how would he know what agriculture and sericulture are? Unless he is of exceptional, godlike intelligence and entrusts affairs to the right men, then with the Eight Delicacies set before him, the Nine Imperial Concubines attending him, and the multitudes of the four quarters and six directions subject to him as servants and concubines to be commanded by a nod of the chin or a glance, at the highest level he will exhaustively seek Penglai and smelt gold and stone, wearing out the realm with things that can never be attained; at the next level he will erect bronze pillars and race heavenly horses, exhausting the strength of the common people to contend for territories that need not be possessed and to subjugate peoples who need never be made subjects; and at the lowest level he will pursue the Three Vices, cast aside the millions of people like a useless cap, and indulge in extreme luxury and utmost…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
皇上御文華殿
親書大字
賜輔臣九卿講官正字官各一幅謝表萬曆二
年
何兆湖
同考試官訓導劉批藻思麗詞悉中矩度且
鋪張我
皇上嘉惠臣工宛然虞廷作歌交儆氣象宜錄以傳
考試官訓導唐批典則得體
===
考試官敎諭鄭批莊麗
萬曆二年某月某日具官臣某等伏蒙
皇上御文華殿
親書大字
頒賜謹奉
表稱
謝者伏以
龍文璀璨欣瞻
日月之光
punctuated:
皇上御文華殿，親書大字，賜輔臣、九卿、講官、正字官各一幅謝表（萬曆二年）
何兆湖
同考試官訓導劉批：藻思麗詞，悉中矩度。且鋪張我皇上嘉惠臣工，宛然虞廷作歌交儆氣象，宜錄以傳。
考試官訓導唐批：典則得體。
考試官敎諭鄭批：莊麗。
萬曆二年某月某日，具官臣某等，伏蒙皇上御文華殿，親書大字頒賜，謹奉表稱謝者。伏以龍文璀璨，欣瞻日月之光；
translation_en:
A Memorial Expressing Gratitude for His Majesty's Appearing at the Hall of Literary Splendor (Wenhua dian), Personally Writing Large Characters, and Bestowing One Scroll Each Upon the Grand Secretaries, the Nine Chief Ministers, the Lecturers-in-Waiting, and the Collators (Second Year of the Wanli Reign [1574])

He Zhaohu 何兆湖

Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Liu comments: Refined thoughts and beautiful diction, all conforming to the standard rules. Moreover, in setting forth the gracious favor of Our August Emperor toward his officials, it vividly captures the spirit of the court of Shun composing songs of mutual admonition. It ought to be recorded and transmitted.

Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang comments: Classical in standard and fitting in style.

Examiner and Instructor Zheng comments: Dignified and splendid.

On a certain day of a certain month in the second year of the Wanli reign, Your servants, [so-and-so], holding full official titles, having humbly received the favor of His Majesty appearing at the Hall of Literary Splendor, personally writing large characters, and bestowing them upon us, respectfully present this memorial to express our gratitude.

We humbly reflect: The dragon calligraphy shines brilliantly, and we joyfully gaze upon the radiance of the sun and moon; …

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
鳳藻輝煌喜溢章縫之會
闡羲皇之心畫
煥河洛之圖書
制出
特恩誼存交儆臣等誠惶誠恐稽首頓首上言
竊惟點畫成文蒼頡顯字書之跡明良交
泰唐虞彰喜起之風商宗夢卜於築巖望
隆舟楫周室矢音于鳴鳳治比圭璋自協
衷之義既微而一體之情遂隔十行一札
===
徒夸恭儉之文玉署商霖未著箴規之訓
自非神明巧悟疇能墨妙臻奇若復上下
情暌安得都俞濟美歷稽往迹未若
今時兹蓋伏遇
皇帝陛下
堯文有煥
舜孝重華
雅崇三事之臣
夙慎六卿之選
punctuated: 鳳藻輝煌，喜溢章縫之會。闡羲皇之心畫，煥河洛之圖書。制出特恩，誼存交儆。臣等誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首上言：竊惟點畫成文，蒼頡顯字書之跡；明良交泰，唐虞彰喜起之風。商宗夢卜於築巖，望隆舟楫；周室矢音于鳴鳳，治比圭璋。自協衷之義既微，而一體之情遂隔。十行一札，徒夸恭儉之文；玉署商霖，未著箴規之訓。自非神明巧悟，疇能墨妙臻奇？若復上下情暌，安得都俞濟美？歷稽往迹，未若今時。兹蓋伏遇皇帝陛下：堯文有煥，舜孝重華。雅崇三事之臣，夙慎六卿之選。
translation_en:
…and the phoenix-like imperial compositions shine with splendor, filling this gathering of scholars in ceremonial robes with overflowing joy. They expound the mind-drawings of the august Fuxi and give new brilliance to the Yellow River Chart and the Luo River Writing. This imperial creation issues from extraordinary grace, yet its meaning abides in mutual admonition between ruler and minister.

Your servants, in utmost awe and trepidation, bow our heads to the ground and humbly submit these words: We venture to reflect that when dots and strokes were formed into writing, Cangjie manifested the traces of scripted characters; when an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers met in harmonious rapport, the eras of Tang and Yu displayed the spirit of joyful and rousing song. High Ancestor of Shang dreamed and divined of the builder at傅巖 (Fuyan), placing in him lofty hopes as his boat and oars; the House of Zhou set forth its verses on the singing phoenix, likening men of governance to jade tablets and scepters.

Yet once the principle of harmonizing the inner minds of ruler and subject grew faint, the sentiment of sharing a single body became estranged. Letters of ten lines on a single tablet merely boasted of polite and frugal phrases; the "Rain of Shang" plaque bestowed on the Jade Hall did not set forth instructions of admonition and regulation. Unless one possesses godlike intelligence and wondrous insight, who could attain the miraculous in the subtleties of ink? And if the sentiments of superior and inferior are alienated, how could they achieve the beauty of agreeing and assenting in counsel? Examining the traces of the past one by one, none can compare with the present age.

This is because we have humbly encountered Your Majesty the Emperor, whose civil pattern shines like that of Yao, and whose filial piety redoubles the splendor of Shun. You ever esteem the ministers of the Three Affairs, and have long exercised care in selecting the Six Ministers…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
陳善責難切殷王三命以聽納逮于正字
勉之敬畏亦以運筆先於治心二十餘紙
揮毫而妙畫天然八十餘字
迎穎而奇鋒手應驚鴻矯鳳擬筆勢之飛翻
周鼎商彝象體裁之莊重然且
文昭是訓
義著作忠儼垂戶牖之銘
寵賁絲綸之指臣等仰觀心悚恭視驩騰爭傳
曠世之奇共羨不期之遇所愧雕龍思乏
===
窺豹才難日侍直于
鑾坡寧堪視草時顧瞻乎
玉簡末稱濡毫猥承
睿藻之輝徒切揄揚之願敢不竭其魯鈍奉以
蓍龜疑丞師保恒觸目以興思
左右阿衡永書紳而圖報班聯
三殿能忘夙夜之在公位列九官誓作百寮
之帥正
螭頭啓沃勉竊附於從繩作礪之風藝苑專
punctuated: 陳善責難，切殷王三命以聽納；逮于正字，勉之敬畏，亦以運筆先於治心。二十餘紙揮毫而妙畫天然，八十餘字迎穎而奇鋒手應。驚鴻矯鳳，擬筆勢之飛翻；周鼎商彝，象體裁之莊重。然且文昭是訓，義著作忠；儼垂戶牖之銘，寵賁絲綸之指。臣等仰觀心悚，恭視驩騰；爭傳曠世之奇，共羨不期之遇。所愧雕龍思乏，窺豹才難。日侍直于鑾坡，寧堪視草；時顧瞻乎玉簡，末稱濡毫。猥承睿藻之輝，徒切揄揚之願。敢不竭其魯鈍，奉以蓍龜？疑丞師保，恒觸目以興思；左右阿衡，永書紳而圖報。班聯三殿，能忘夙夜之在公？位列九官，誓作百寮之帥正。螭頭啓沃，勉竊附於從繩作礪之風；藝苑專…
translation_en: …setting forth the good and reproving what is difficult, earnestly following the three charges of the Yin king in listening and accepting; and when coming to the correction of characters, urging reverence and awe, likewise holding that governing the mind precedes wielding the brush. Across more than twenty sheets Your Majesty flourished the brush, and the marvelous strokes were naturally formed; in over eighty characters the brush tip met the paper, and wondrous points answered the hand. Startled wild geese and soaring phoenixes may be likened to the flying sweep of the brushwork; Zhou tripods and Shang ritual vessels image the grave dignity of its form and style. Moreover, its resplendent writing serves as instruction, and its manifest meaning encourages loyalty; it hangs majestically like inscriptions on doors and windows, and graciously adorns the purport of Your silken words of decree. Your servants look up at it with awe in our hearts, and gaze upon it reverently with leaping joy; we vie to pass on this marvel rare in any age, and together admire an encounter beyond all expectation. What shames us is that we lack the thought for carving dragons, and hardly possess the talent that glimpses even a spot of the leopard. Attending on daily duty at the Slope of the Imperial Bells, how could we be worthy of drafting decrees? Gazing from time to time upon the jade tablets, we are scarcely fit to moisten the brush. Having undeservedly received the radiance of Your imperial compositions, we merely harbor an earnest wish to extol and praise them. How dare we not exhaust our dullness and revere them as yarrow stalks and tortoise shells for divination? As Doubter, Assistant, Preceptor, and Guardian, whenever our eyes light upon them we shall be stirred to reflection; as flanking ministers like Aheng, we shall forever write them upon our sashes and seek to repay Your grace. Standing in the court ranks of the Three Great Halls, how could we forget to be at our public duties early and late? Placed among the Nine Offices, we vow to serve as upright leaders for all the hundred officials. Offering counsel beside the dragon-head carvings, we shall strive humbly to attach ourselves to the ethos of following the marking-line and serving as a whetstone; in the garden of letters devoting our…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
精將一洗乎魯魚亥豕之謬伏願
至誠無息
上德益謙
省觀不替夫風愆
顧諟無忘于日監
率乃攸行紹
二祖
八宗爲太平之
天子
===
念惟典學同天長地久稱有道之
聖人臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹奉
表稱
謝以
聞
第叁場
策〔五道〕
punctuated:
精，將一洗乎魯魚亥豕之謬。伏願至誠無息，上德益謙，省觀不替夫風愆，顧諟無忘于日監，率乃攸行，紹二祖、八宗爲太平之天子；念惟典學，同天長地久稱有道之聖人。臣等無任瞻天仰聖、激切屏營之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

第叁場
策〔五道〕
translation_en:
… [dedicating our] utmost focus, we shall thoroughly sweep away the copying errors of mistaking *lu* for *yu* or *hai* for *shi*.

We humbly pray that with unceasing utmost sincerity and supreme virtue grown ever more modest, You will never relax Your self-examination against faults warned of by the winds, nor forget in Your contemplation of Heaven's clear mandate that it watches over You daily; that by following the path of Your predecessors, You will continue the line of the Two Progenitors and Eight Ancestors as a Son of Heaven of Grand Peace; and that by ever fixing Your thoughts on canonical learning, You will be acclaimed for as long as Heaven and Earth endure as a Sage of the True Way.

Your servants, overwhelmed with emotion and reverent trepidation as we look up to Heaven and gaze upon Your Sagely Majesty, respectfully present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's hearing.

Third Session
Policy Essays [Five Questions]

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
第一問
吳國光
同考試官教諭楊批對揚
皇上心學而篇末歸重府部敷陳尤見忠懇
考試官訓導唐批論
聖學歸於大本大原有見
考試官教諭鄭批對揚殆盡
古之聖帝明王所以致盛治隆大業者必
係於所養養之云者非以其億兆之推奉
===
也端玄居尊以天下恣睢也養之以德而
成之以學學以經政則不泥政以適時則
不盭由是恭巳而成功淵默以待治則理
道歸焉矣故廣厦細旃左圖右史非以飾
觀也而澄本之要實具焉遠取三五近取
季叔雌黄是非非以飾議也而理道之務
實存焉六曹之封駁九官之獻替五兵七
校之條列非以瀆其納聽也而經畫之權
寓焉今之
punctuated:
第一問
吳國光
同考試官教諭楊批：對揚皇上心學，而篇末歸重府部敷陳，尤見忠懇。
考試官訓導唐批：論聖學歸於大本大原，有見。
考試官教諭鄭批：對揚殆盡。

古之聖帝明王，所以致盛治、隆大業者，必係於所養。養之云者，非以其億兆之推奉也，端玄居尊，以天下恣睢也；養之以德，而成之以學。學以經政則不泥，政以適時則不盭。由是恭巳而成功，淵默以待治，則理道歸焉矣。故廣厦細旃，左圖右史，非以飾觀也，而澄本之要實具焉；遠取三五，近取季叔，雌黄是非，非以飾議也，而理道之務實存焉；六曹之封駁，九官之獻替，五兵七校之條列，非以瀆其納聽也，而經畫之權寓焉。今之
translation_en:
First Question
Wu Guoguang 吳國光
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Yang: He responds by extolling His Majesty's learning of the mind-and-heart, and at the end of the piece places the ultimate emphasis on the exposition by the Chief Military Commissions and the Ministries, which especially shows his loyalty and sincerity.
Comment by Examiner and Assistant Instructor Tang: In discussing sagely learning, he traces it back to the great root and great source; this shows insight.
Comment by Examiner and Instructor Zheng: His response extols the theme almost exhaustively.

The means by which the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity brought about flourishing governance and exalted their great enterprises invariably depended upon what they nourished. What is meant by "nourishing" is not that, because of the veneration and support of the millions of people, they sat in solemn mystery in the position of supreme honor and did whatever they pleased with the realm; rather, they nourished themselves with virtue and brought it to completion through learning. When learning is used to regulate governance, it does not become bogged down in rigidity; when governance is adapted to the times, it does not go awry. Consequently, by maintaining reverent self-restraint they achieved success, and by remaining in deep silence they awaited good order, so that the principles of governance naturally converged in them. Therefore, sitting on fine felt rugs in spacious halls, with charts to the left and histories to the right, is not meant merely to adorn appearances, for the essentials of clarifying the fundamental root are truly present therein; drawing remotely from the Three Emperors and Five Sovereigns and drawing recently from later ages, revising and evaluating right and wrong, is not meant merely to embellish discussion, for the urgent tasks of the principles of governance truly exist therein; the sealed critiques and vetoes of the Six Offices, the counsel and remonstrance of the Nine Officials, and the itemized reports of the Five Armies and Seven Regiments are not meant to importune the sovereign's receptive hearing, for the authority of planning and management resides therein. title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
經筵備是矣而執事猶謂君心惟在所養欲
求其大本大原之所在無亦以諸生之中
有能識政學之要者與夫養之道難言也
今之所謂養者不過曰八珍九鼎所以養
口也椒蘭芬茝所以養氣也大輅越席所
以養體也錯衡和鸞所以養聲也然皆晚
近世之所務而上世之所後也董子所謂
正心以正朝廷學禮之所謂五學成於上
百姓化於下是聖王之所事而不徒章句
===
耳矣故切而不愧化與心成而治紀係之
吾得殷宗之說命焉其曰霖雨之於旱也
礪之於金也舟楫之於巨川也鹽梅之於
和羹也股肱之於人也伊湯之以託諷也
而究本於輔德沃心率屬匡辟蓋理人之
大機統之君子謂殷宗以政爲學也其指
要管是矣自漢以來蓋寥寥焉石渠講論
名儒召集吾得宣帝而恭顯方士得以伺
其隙則已雜於支岐矣臨雍拜老諸儒執
punctuated: 經筵備是矣。而執事猶謂「君心惟在所養」，欲求其大本大原之所在，無亦以諸生之中有能識政學之要者與？夫養之道，難言也。今之所謂養者，不過曰：八珍九鼎，所以養口也；椒蘭芬茝，所以養氣也；大輅越席，所以養體也；錯衡和鸞，所以養聲也。然皆晚近世之所務，而上世之所後也。董子所謂「正心以正朝廷」，《學禮》之所謂「五學成於上，百姓化於下」，是聖王之所事，而不徒章句耳矣。故切而不愧，化與心成，而治紀係之，吾得殷宗之《說命》焉。其曰霖雨之於旱也，礪之於金也，舟楫之於巨川也，鹽梅之於和羹也，股肱之於人也，伊、湯之以託諷也，而究本於輔德沃心、率屬匡辟，蓋理人之大機統之。君子謂「殷宗以政爲學」也，其指要管是矣。自漢以來，蓋寥寥焉。石渠講論，名儒召集，吾得宣帝；而恭、顯、方士得以伺其隙，則已雜於支岐矣。臨雍拜老，諸儒執
translation_en:
… Classics Colloquium is already fully equipped with all of these. Yet you, Sir, still say that "the ruler's mind depends solely on how it is nourished," and wish to seek out where its great foundation and great source lie—is it not because you think there may be among us students someone capable of recognizing the essentials of governance and learning?

Now, the way of nourishing is difficult to speak of. What is called "nourishing" nowadays amounts to nothing more than saying: the eight delicacies and nine tripods are wherewith to nourish the mouth; pepper, orchid, and fragrant angelica are wherewith to nourish the vital breath; the grand carriage and woven reed mats are wherewith to nourish the body; and the ornamented yoke-bar and harmonious bells are wherewith to nourish the ear for sound. Yet all of these are what later, recent ages have busied themselves with, and what high antiquity put last. What Master Dong [Dong Zhongshu] called "rectifying the mind in order to rectify the court," and what the Rituals of Learning (Xueli) calls "when the five learnings are perfected above, the common people are transformed below"—this is what the sage-kings devoted themselves to, and it was not a matter of mere chapter-and-verse scholarship!

Therefore, for being earnest and without cause for shame, where transformation is achieved together with the mind and the threads of governance are bound up with it, I find the "Charge to Yue" (Shuoming) of High Ancestor Gaozong of Yin. What it says about timely rain in a drought, a whetstone to metal, boats and oars to a great river, salt and plum to a well-blended soup, and limbs to a person—such were the allegories by which Yi Yin and Tang conveyed remonstrance [?], yet ultimately it is rooted in assisting virtue and enriching the heart-mind, leading the subordinates and rectifying the sovereign, for the great mechanism of governing others is unified therein. When the gentleman says that "the Yin ancestor took governance as his learning," its essential import is summed up right here.

Since the Han dynasty, such examples have been few and far between. Holding discussions in the Stone Canal Pavilion (Shiqu ge) and summoning renowned Confucians—there I find Emperor Xuan; yet Hong Gong, Shi Xian, and the masters of esoterica (fangshi) were able to spy out his vulnerabilities, so his learning was already adulterated by side paths. Visiting the Biyong Hall to pay respects to the aged, while the various Confucians held…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
經吾得明帝而鍾離宋均以察慧言則巳
傷於苛細矣弘文置館考定五經太宗之
學似矣而大綱未正如貞觀之鮮終何崇
政說書累幸太學仁宗之學勤矣而吏治
蝓惰如天聖之微瑕何是數君者或博覽
而不究義理或書史而無關身心蓋自殷
宗以後之事殆難言之矣洪惟我
太祖高皇帝提三尺埽胡元闢乾
御寓天下旣定戢藏干戈講究經藝隨在有得
===
觀其聽宋濂講大學而喜爲治平之要朱
善講周易而悟家人之指許存仁講洪範
而推庶徵之義其曰帝治莫隆於堯舜則
謨典之精也曰人心莫嚴於氣機則日躋
之敬也曰文章莫要於經世則訓誥之略
也曰爲君畏天地兆民則六馬之馭也
列聖相承
紹休趾美仰惟
成祖悟峻德於大學揭性善於講說非其學之
punctuated: 經，吾得明帝，而鍾離、宋均以察慧言，則巳傷於苛細矣。弘文置館，考定《五經》，太宗之學似矣，而大綱未正，如貞觀之鮮終何？崇政說書，累幸太學，仁宗之學勤矣，而吏治蝓惰，如天聖之微瑕何？是數君者，或博覽而不究義理，或書史而無關身心，蓋自殷宗以後之事，殆難言之矣。洪惟我太祖高皇帝提三尺埽胡元，闢乾御寓，天下旣定，戢藏干戈，講究經藝，隨在有得。觀其聽宋濂講《大學》，而喜爲治平之要；朱善講《周易》，而悟《家人》之指；許存仁講《洪範》，而推庶徵之義。其曰：「帝治莫隆於堯、舜」，則謨、典之精也；曰：「人心莫嚴於氣機」，則日躋之敬也；曰：「文章莫要於經世」，則訓、誥之略也；曰：「爲君畏天地兆民」，則六馬之馭也。列聖相承，紹休趾美。仰惟成祖悟峻德於《大學》，揭性善於講說，非其學之
translation_en:
… the Classics, we find in Emperor Ming [of Han]; yet Zhongli [Yi 鍾離意] and Song Jun 宋均 spoke of his astute scrutinizing, which shows it was already marred by petty fussiness. Establishing the Institute for the Advancement of Literature (Hongwen guan) and examining and fixing the texts of the Five Classics—the learning of Taizong [of Tang] seemed genuine enough; yet the great fundamental principles were not rectified, so what could be done about the failure of the Zhenguan reign to end well? Expounding books in the Hall of Venerating Governance (Chongzheng dian) and repeatedly visiting the National University—the learning of Renzong [of Song] was diligent enough; yet official administration grew lax and sluggish, so what could be done about the slight flaws of the Tiansheng reign? Among these several rulers, some read widely without investigating moral principles, while others studied books and histories without connecting them to self-cultivation and the mind. Indeed, what transpired after the high ancestors of Yin is scarcely worth speaking of!

We reflect with awe upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), who wielded a three-foot sword to sweep away the barbarian Yuan, opened up Heaven's order and ruled the realm. Once the empire was settled, he put away weapons of war, expounded and investigated the Classics and arts, and gained insight wherever he turned. Observe how, listening to Song Lian 宋濂 lecture on the Great Learning (Daxue), he rejoiced in it as the essential way to govern and bring peace; when Zhu Shan 朱善 lectured on the Book of Changes (Zhouyi), he grasped the purport of the "Family" (Jiaren) hexagram; when Xu Cunren 許存仁 lectured on the "Great Plan" (Hongfan), he extended the meaning of the "various verifications" (shuzheng). When he said, "Imperial governance was never more exalted than under Yao and Shun," this was the essence of the "Counsels" and "Canons" [of the Book of Documents]; when he said, "Nothing in the human mind requires stricter guard than the subtle springs of vital force (qiji)," this was the reverence that "ascends daily" [of King Tang in the Book of Odes]; when he said, "In writing, nothing is more essential than ordering the world," this was the grand strategy of the "Instructions" and "Announcements" [of the Book of Documents]; and when he said, "To be a ruler is to stand in awe of Heaven, Earth, and the millions of the people," this was the driving of six horses [with rotten reins, from the Book of Documents].

Successive sacred emperors have carried on the heritage, continuing its splendors and following in its noble footsteps. Looking up in reverence, we reflect upon how Chengzu awakened to "lofty virtue" in the Great Learning and held up the goodness of human nature in his lectures and explanations—was not his learning…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
自得師者乎
仁宗覽正宗而辨學取三經之直指非其學之
先體要者乎於大學而知財用於豳風而
念稼穡在
宣宗之心法可想也羨嘉言於典謨悟治安於
講讀在
英宗之心法可窺也以至
文華大訓之書綱目續編之史
敬一有箴
===
心箴有註又我
憲宗
世宗之意緒所存而足以軼邁乎三五之遺烈
者矣此豈徒獵篇籍以博見聞習藻繪以
飾偉儀也哉
皇上
睿質天授
英悟夙成當
訪落之年
punctuated:
自得師者乎？仁宗覽《正宗》而辨學，取《三經》之直指，非其學之先體要者乎？於《大學》而知財用，於《豳風》而念稼穡，在宣宗之心法可想也。羨嘉言於典謨，悟治安於講讀，在英宗之心法可窺也。以至《文華大訓》之書、《綱目續編》之史，《敬一》有箴、《心箴》有註，又我憲宗、世宗之意緒所存，而足以軼邁乎三五之遺烈者矣。此豈徒獵篇籍以博見聞、習藻繪以飾偉儀也哉？

皇上睿質天授，英悟夙成，當訪落之年，
translation_en:
…finding a teacher within oneself? When Emperor Renzong perused the Orthodox Tradition (Zhengzong) to discern learning, and adopted the direct explanations of the Three Classics, was this not putting the essential substance first in his learning? From the Great Learning (Daxue) he understood fiscal resources, and from the "Airs of Bin" ("Binfeng") he was mindful of sowing and reaping—in these, the method of the mind of Emperor Xuanzong can be imagined. Admiring fine words in the Canons and Counsels, and grasping peace and order through lectures and readings—in these, the method of the mind of Emperor Yingzong can be glimpsed. Extending further to the book Great Instructions of the Wenhua Hall (Wenhua daxun) and the history Sequel to the Outline and Details (Gangmu xubian), as well as the Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi zhen) and the commentary on the Admonition on the Mind (Xinzhen), these again are where the intentions and threads of thought of our Emperors Xianzong and Shizong reside, sufficient to surpass the lingering achievements of the Three Kings and Five Emperors. How could this merely be skimming through texts to broaden one's knowledge, or practicing ornate rhetoric to embellish a grand demeanor?

His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with sagely qualities and achieved brilliant comprehension early in life. At the age of consulting his ministers upon ascending the throne,…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
邁師古之志
講幃不輟
御墳典不輟究緝熈
聖學直有以遠邁殷宗而上之愚獨以為
帝王之學與韋布不同在尋究指歸而不在侈
靡在提挈綱領而不在涉獵雖考究往古
而不可不閱歷世務雖敷求前哲而不可
不達知民情五府之軍政有成列矣而九
邊將領伍符尺籍獨不可因間而條其精
===
脃以振惕之乎冢宰之考績有
成憲矣而調補署置分曹計吏獨不可因間而
別其殿最以科條之乎司徒之歲會有常
數矣而戶口阨塞贏縮息耗獨不可因間
而制其緩急以均節之乎宗伯之於禮司
馬之於兵固各有司存矣而臚颺封拜擇
將籌邊又不可不敷陳搉確以推移於權
變者也司寇之於刑司空之於土固各有
職守矣而平亭操縱地利物力又不可不
punctuated: 邁師古之志，講幃不輟，御墳典不輟，究緝熈聖學，直有以遠邁殷宗而上之。愚獨以為帝王之學與韋布不同，在尋究指歸而不在侈靡，在提挈綱領而不在涉獵。雖考究往古，而不可不閱歷世務；雖敷求前哲，而不可不達知民情。五府之軍政有成列矣，而九邊將領、伍符尺籍，獨不可因間而條其精脃以振惕之乎？冢宰之考績有成憲矣，而調補署置、分曹計吏，獨不可因間而別其殿最以科條之乎？司徒之歲會有常數矣，而戶口阨塞、贏縮息耗，獨不可因間而制其緩急以均節之乎？宗伯之於禮，司馬之於兵，固各有司存矣，而臚颺封拜、擇將籌邊，又不可不敷陳搉確以推移於權變者也。司寇之於刑，司空之於土，固各有職守矣，而平亭操縱、地利物力，又不可不
translation_en: …[Right from the years when Your Majesty first consulted with Your ministers upon ascending the throne, You] have surpassed others in Your aspiration to take antiquity as Your teacher. At the lecture curtain You have been unceasing; in perusing the ancient canons You have been unceasing. In investigating and continuing the radiant sagely learning, You truly have the wherewithal to far surpass the high kings of Yin and ascend even above them. Yet in my humble opinion, the learning of an emperor or king differs from that of a commoner in coarse cloth: it lies in investigating the essential import rather than in extravagant elaboration, and in grasping the overarching principles rather than in superficial browsing. Although one examines remote antiquity, one must not fail to experience the affairs of the world; although one broadly seeks out the former wise men, one must not fail to thoroughly understand the conditions of the people. The military administration of the Five Chief Military Commissions is already arranged in established order; yet as for the commanders of the Nine Defense Commands, the squad tallies, and the military registers, could one not take advantage of moments of leisure to itemize their strengths and weaknesses so as to rouse them to vigilance? The evaluation of official merit by the Minister of Personnel already has established statutes; yet as for transfers, appointments, and the assessment of officials across the various bureaus, could one not take advantage of moments of leisure to distinguish the lowest from the highest ranks and regulate them by category? The annual fiscal accounts of the Minister of Revenue already have regular quotas; yet as for the strategic passes and household registration, and the surpluses, deficits, growth, and depletion, could one not take advantage of moments of leisure to determine what is urgent and what is secondary so as to equalize and moderate them? The Minister of Rites with respect to ceremonies, and the Minister of War with respect to military affairs, indeed each have their designated offices; yet when it comes to proclaiming investitures and appointments, or selecting generals and planning frontier defense, these too must not fail to be set forth and thoroughly deliberated upon, so as to adapt to changing circumstances. The Minister of Justice with respect to punishments, and the Minister of Works with respect to public lands and works, indeed each have their official duties; yet when it comes to adjudicating with fairness and exercising leniency or strictness, or utilizing the advantages of the terrain and material resources, these too must not fail to…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
敷陳參酌以節適於時幾者也凡此皆
祖宗法度與墳典相出入論學經政與直講相
為用而不徒限局迷遠拘玄妨素以屑屑
於詞章者矣昔者蘇軾程頤之於哲宗也
或反覆開導或莊嚴諷諫要不出就事論
事納約自牖即今之所論政學可為後世
法程至明也但
朝廷日有
萬幾
===
法宮遠於天上簾堂之勢隔臣
主之分嚴道古則病於迂徐談今則傷於瑣細
難乎相悅以解也然學在資人道在師心
得其心則三風十愆莫非成訓眷求其人
則四墉九主莫非儀刑矣說命曰非知之
艱行之惟艱王忱不艱允協先王成德蓋
聰明聖智者戒於自用廣聞博取者戒於
近名故審其所以戒而勉其所以行則可
以邁德殷宗而繩休
punctuated: 敷陳參酌，以節適於時幾者也。凡此皆祖宗法度與墳典相出入，論學經政與直講相為用，而不徒限局迷遠、拘玄妨素，以屑屑於詞章者矣。昔者蘇軾、程頤之於哲宗也，或反覆開導，或莊嚴諷諫，要不出就事論事、納約自牖，即今之所論政學，可為後世法程，至明也。但朝廷日有萬幾，法宮遠於天上，簾堂之勢隔，臣主之分嚴，道古則病於迂徐，談今則傷於瑣細，難乎相悅以解也。然學在資人，道在師心。得其心，則三風十愆莫非成訓；眷求其人，則四墉九主莫非儀刑矣。《說命》曰：「非知之艱，行之惟艱。王忱不艱，允協先王成德。」蓋聰明聖智者戒於自用，廣聞博取者戒於近名，故審其所以戒而勉其所以行，則可以邁德殷宗，而繩休
translation_en:
…be set forth and weighed together so as to be regulated and adapted to the exigencies of the moment. In all these matters, the laws and institutions of our Imperial Ancestors move in and out in harmony with the ancient classics and canons, and discussions of learning and the management of governance serve mutually with direct lectures in the Classics Colloquium—rather than merely confining oneself within narrow bounds while losing sight of what is far-reaching, or clinging to abstruse subtleties to the detriment of plain substance by busying oneself overmere literary phrasing.

In former times, when Su Shi 蘇軾 and Cheng Yi 程頤 served Emperor Zhezong 哲宗, whether through repeated and patient guidance or through solemn remonstrance, the essential point never went beyond discussing matters on the basis of the concrete affairs at hand and introducing concise counsel through whatever opening presented itself. That is precisely what is being discussed today as governance and learning, and it is crystal clear that this can serve as a standard and model for later generations.

However, the Court attends daily to ten thousand affairs of state, the Imperial Palace is as distant as the heavens above, the majesty of the throne hall creates a barrier, and the distinction between minister and sovereign is strict. To speak of antiquity is faulted as circuitous and slow; to discuss the present is criticized as trivial and petty—how difficult it is to achieve mutual delight and true understanding! Yet learning lies in drawing upon others, and the Way lies in taking the mind as one's teacher. Once one grasps this mind, then even the warnings against the "three decadent winds and ten faults" are all established instructions; once one earnestly seeks out such men, then the "four walls" of ministerial support and the lessons of the "nine types of rulers" are all models of conduct.

The "Charge to Yue" (Shuoming 說命) says: "It is not knowing that is difficult, it is acting that is惟 difficult. If the King's sincerity finds no difficulty in action, he will truly accord with the accomplished virtue of the former kings." Indeed, those of keen intelligence and sage wisdom must guard against relying solely on themselves, and those of wide learning and broad selection must guard against seeking mere reputation. Therefore, if the sovereign examines what he must guard against and exerts himself in what he must put into practice, he can surpass the virtue of the high sovereigns of Yin and continue the glorious…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
祖武不然則日之孜孜陳對者未有不以為土
苴贅疣也雖然飛坒之微不益華嶽涓滴
之潤何裨江河然而有需焉者取益無擇
也夫學之道持心難慎終尤難蓋上智不
能無欲而小人巧於伺間况以
天子之尊臨之以環向待命之衆脫声□語千
里響應一有不慎安知不中之神仙土木
方士狗馬以侈靡其心者漢之武宣宋之
真神其明鑑也故知所以持心又知所以
===
慎終資公孤之弼亮究宮諭之誦規考六
卿之質成察臺省之獻納跡六代之興替
監
祖宗之建立而又昭無欲之路博和睦之化明
自然之道覽六藝之意酌虞夏之質文定
殷周之損益不徒以侈彌文耀觀聽棄華
取實則天下曉然知
聖學之所在大化可成禮讓可興即三五之隆
何以加諸
punctuated: 祖武。不然，則日之孜孜陳對者，未有不以為土苴贅疣也。雖然，飛坒之微，不益華嶽；涓滴之潤，何裨江河？然而有需焉者，取益無擇也。夫學之道，持心難，慎終尤難。蓋上智不能無欲，而小人巧於伺間，况以天子之尊，臨之以環向待命之衆，脫声□語，千里響應。一有不慎，安知不中之神仙、土木、方士、狗馬，以侈靡其心者？漢之武、宣，宋之真、神，其明鑑也。故知所以持心，又知所以慎終。資公孤之弼亮，究宮諭之誦規，考六卿之質成，察臺省之獻納，跡六代之興替，監祖宗之建立，而又昭無欲之路，博和睦之化，明自然之道，覽六藝之意，酌虞夏之質文，定殷周之損益，不徒以侈彌文、耀觀聽，棄華取實，則天下曉然知聖學之所在，大化可成，禮讓可興，即三五之隆，何以加諸？
translation_en:
… footsteps of the imperial ancestors. Otherwise, those who diligently present their replies day after day would without exception be regarded as mere dregs and superfluous excrescences. Even so, the minuteness of flying dust adds nothing to Mount Hua, and the moisture of a tiny drop is of what benefit to the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers? Yet the reason there is still a need for them is that in drawing benefit, one makes no exclusions.

Now, in the Way of learning, maintaining the mind is difficult, and being careful to the very end is even more difficult. For even those of the highest wisdom cannot be entirely free of desires, while petty men are clever at spying out openings. How much more so when, from the exalted position of the Son of Heaven, one presides over a multitude facing him from all around awaiting his commands, where a single uttered sound or [?] word is echoed for a thousand li! If there is a single lapse in caution, how can one know that they will not strike at his vulnerability with immortals, building projects, occultists, and hounds and horses to make his mind extravagant and dissipated? Emperors Wu and Xuan of the Han, and Emperors Zhenzong and Shenzong of the Song, are clear mirrors of this.

Therefore, when one knows how to maintain the mind and also knows how to be careful to the end—relying on the assistance and guidance of the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries, investigating the admonitory recitations of the Palace Lecturers, examining the verified achievements of the Six Ministers, heeding the advice submitted by the Censorate and the Ministries, tracing the rise and fall of the Six Dynasties, taking the institutions established by the Imperial Ancestors as a mirror, and furthermore manifesting the path of desirelessness, broadening the transformation of harmony, clarifying the Way of spontaneity, surveying the meaning of the Six Arts, weighing the substance and refinement of Yu and Xia, and determining what to abbreviate or augment from Yin and Zhou, not merely indulging in elaborate formalities to dazzle the eyes and ears of observers, but discarding华华 superficiality and choosing substance—then the whole empire will clearly know wherein Sacred Learning lies. Great moral transformation can be achieved, ritual propriety and deference can be revived, and even the flourishing height of the Three Kings and Five Emperors—how could it surpass this?

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
第二問
黃希奭
同考試官訓導唐批學術事功一原即漢唐
宋諸賢各有所得子獨闡明詳盡考據精確而末
段尤見尚友之志取之
考試官訓導唐批學術事功原非二物世
儒岐而二之蓋未之深體也是作俯仰品騭得其
源委異日必能推學建功者取之
考試官敎諭鄭批辨博峻整
===
夫所稱於天下爲大儒者必有振古之學
術而後有振古之事功要之學術事功非
二也古之學者天地之變動日月星辰之
運行萬物之散聚山川谿谷之險易阨塞
皇帝王伯之汙隆與夫墳典丘索陰符揣
摩奇正權變靡不習貫而用之以正出之
以時故雖勇奪三軍而不攘臂於睚眦之
小智蓋天下而不角勝於閭伍之間辯屈
羣策而不輕試於脣吻之末力高一世而
punctuated:
第二問
黃希奭
同考試官訓導唐批：「學術事功一原，即漢、唐、宋諸賢各有所得，子獨闡明詳盡，考據精確，而末段尤見尚友之志。取之。」
考試官訓導唐批：「學術事功原非二物，世儒岐而二之，蓋未之深體也。是作俯仰品騭，得其源委，異日必能推學建功者。取之。」
考試官敎諭鄭批：「辨博峻整。」

夫所稱於天下爲大儒者，必有振古之學術，而後有振古之事功。要之，學術、事功非二也。古之學者，天地之變動，日月星辰之運行，萬物之散聚，山川谿谷之險易阨塞，皇、帝、王、伯之汙隆，與夫《墳》、《典》、《丘》、《索》、《陰符》、《揣摩》，奇正權變，靡不習貫，而用之以正，出之以時。故雖勇奪三軍，而不攘臂於睚眦之小；智蓋天下，而不角勝於閭伍之間；辯屈羣策，而不輕試於脣吻之末；力高一世，而
translation_en:
Second Policy Question
Huang Xishi 黃希奭
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Tang comments: "Scholarship and practical achievement share a single origin. Though the various worthies of the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties each attained something of it, you alone have elucidated this exhaustively with precise and accurate evidential grounding, and the final section especially reveals an aspiration to befriend the ancients. Accepted."
Examiner Assistant Instructor Tang comments: "Scholarship and practical achievement are originally not two separate things; vulgar Confucians of the world divide them into two because they have not deeply embodied them. Looking up and down through history, this essay evaluates and ranks its subjects, grasping their origins and developments. In the future, the author will surely be one capable of extending his learning to establish achievements. Accepted."
Examiner Instructor Zheng comments: "Eloquent, erudite, lofty, and well-ordered."

Now, those who are acclaimed throughout the empire as great Confucians must first possess scholarship that resonates through antiquity before they can achieve practical deeds that resonate through antiquity. In sum, scholarship and practical achievement are not two separate things. As for the scholars of antiquity—the transformations and movements of Heaven and Earth; the revolutions of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations; the dispersion and gathering of the myriad things; the strategic passes, difficulties, and ease of mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys; the decline and flourishing of the August Ones, Emperors, Kings, and Hegemons; as well as the Three Mounds (Sanfen), Five Canons (Wudian), Eight索 (Basuo), Nine邱 (Jiuqiu), the Secret Tally (Yinfu), and the Art of Gauging Minds (Chuaimo), along with the unorthodox and orthodox, and expediency and adaptation—there was nothing they did not thoroughly master, yet they employed this knowledge with rectitude and brought it forth according to the proper time. Therefore, although their courage could outmatch the Three Armies, they would not roll up their sleeves over petty grievances; although their wisdom covered the empire, they would not vie for victory among village lanes; although their eloquence could bend all other counsels, they would not lightly test it in trivial verbal sparring; although their strength towered over their generation, they…

title: 萬曆七年廣東鄉試錄
text:
不爲舉鼎絶臏之事行必大道有時乎徑
竇可由約誓是尊有時乎要盟不信可經
可權可靜可動尸居而龍見雷聲而淵默
養其全鋒以待天下顧盼呼吸而豎峻偉
不羣之業其發也若機括其炳也若日月
掀揭照耀萬世之所咄嗟慨噫鼓掌而甘
心焉者也乃今之爲學術者好申一隅之
說多謬通方之論貴席上者以清淨爲腐
議束名實者以柱下爲誕詞從橫游談則
===
病其辯譎權謀功利則詆其詭曲吾以爲
才智有偏兼而其致用有遇合要以適時
應變取節焉耳矣夫玉卮無當賤於瓦缶
太阿不割不直鈆刀彼其侈談而無益於
用也何異哉至其語事功則又曰德衰於
符斗信折於繩契爲誕而已矣忠敞於管
晏質破於申韓爲名而已矣噫彼徒知上
古之不符斗不繩契而不知今之民則符
斗繩契之民也知其治之不必管晏申韓
punctuated: 不爲舉鼎絶臏之事。行必大道，有時乎徑竇可由；約誓是尊，有時乎要盟不信。可經可權，可靜可動，尸居而龍見，雷聲而淵默。養其全鋒以待天下，顧盼呼吸，而豎峻偉不羣之業。其發也若機括，其炳也若日月，掀揭照耀，萬世之所咄嗟慨噫、鼓掌而甘心焉者也。乃今之爲學術者，好申一隅之說，多謬通方之論。貴席上者，以清淨爲腐議；束名實者，以柱下爲誕詞。從橫游談，則病其辯譎；權謀功利，則詆其詭曲。吾以爲才智有偏兼，而其致用有遇合，要以適時應變，取節焉耳矣。夫玉卮無當，賤於瓦缶；太阿不割，不直鈆刀。彼其侈談而無益於用也，何異哉？至其語事功，則又曰：「德衰於符斗，信折於繩契，爲誕而已矣；忠敞於管、晏，質破於申、韓，爲名而已矣。」噫！彼徒知上古之不符斗、不繩契，而不知今之民則符斗、繩契之民也；知其治之不必管、晏、申、韓，
translation_en:
… would not engage in feats like lifting a cauldron until one's kneecap snaps. In conduct they surely walked the Great Way, yet at times a shortcut or side opening could be taken; they honored covenants and oaths, yet at times a coerced alliance would not be kept. Able to uphold the standard and able to exercise expediency, able to be still and able to act, they sat motionless like a ceremonial impersonator of the dead yet appeared like a dragon, thundered aloud yet remained silent as an abyss. They nourished their full sharpness to await the needs of the world, and in the glance of an eye or the drawing of a breath, established lofty, magnificent, and extraordinary achievements. Their release was like a crossbow trigger; their brilliance was like the sun and moon—held aloft and shining forth, that over which ten thousand generations exclaim in admiration, sigh in wonder, clap their hands, and find deep satisfaction.

Yet those who pursue learning today are fond of advancing one-sided views and often distort comprehensive principles. Those who prize treasures for the banquet mat [Confucian ritualists] regard quietism and non-action as stale talk; those who bind names to realities [Logicians/Legalists] regard the words of the Archivist Under the Pillar [Laozi] as absurdities. As for the wandering persuaders of vertical and horizontal alliances, they fault them for specious rhetoric; as for tactical schemes and utilitarian gain, they disparage them as deceitful and crooked. In my view, talents and wisdom may be partial or comprehensive, and their practical application depends on opportunity and circumstance; the essential point is simply to suit the times, respond to change, and select what is appropriate in due measure. Now, a jade goblet without a bottom is worth less than an earthen jar; if the great Tai'e sword does not cut, it is not worth a lead knife. How are those who indulge in extravagant talk that is of no benefit to practical use any different?

When they speak of practical achievements, they further say: "Virtue declined with tallies and peck-measures, and trust was broken with knotted cords and notched tallies—all that is mere absurdity; loyalty was ruined by Guan Zhong and Yan Ying, and unadorned substance was shattered by Shen Buhai and Han Fei—all that is mere pursuit of reputation." Alas! They merely know that high antiquity did not use tallies and peck-measures or knotted cords and notched tallies, without realizing that the people of today are indeed a people of tallies, peck-measures, knotted cords, and notched tallies; they know that governance need not rely on Guan Zhong, Yan Ying, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei …
